chunks: Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Masroor (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Aamir narrated to us from his uncle Abdullah ibn Aamir, from Sulayman ibn Hafs al-Marwazi, who said: I heard Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying:

Whoever visits the grave of my son Ali, there will be for him with God the Exalted seventy accepted pilgrimages. I said: Seventy pilgrimages? He said: Yes, and seventy thousand pilgrimages. Then he said: There are many pilgrimages that are not accepted.
And whoever visits him or spends a night next to him is like one who has visited God the Exalted at His Throne. I said: Like one who visited God at His Throne? He said: Yes.

When the Day of Resurrection comes, there will be on the Throne of God, Exalted is His Glory, four from the earlier [prophets] and four from the later [prophets]. As for the first four, they are Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. And as for the other four, they are Muhammad, Ali, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn.
Then the rope will be extended, and the visitors of the graves of the Imams will sit with us. Indeed, those with the highest rank and closest proximity are the visitors of the grave of my son Ali.

The author of this book (may God have mercy on him) said: The meaning of his saying (peace be upon him) 'is like one who visited God at His Throne' is not a physical comparison, because the angels visit the Throne, take refuge in it, and circumambulate around it, and say 'We visit God at His Throne,' just as we say 'We perform Hajj to the House of God' and 'We visit God,' because God the Exalted is not described by a place, Exalted is He with a great elevation.

key_terms.رُبَّ حَجَّةٍ لَا تُقْبَلُ: Many pilgrimages that are not accepted

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual reward of visiting the shrine of Imam Ali ibn Musa al-Rida (a.s.) compared to Hajj?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Uyun Akhbar al-Rida*, Imam Musa al-Kadhim (a.s.) highlights the supreme spiritual status of visiting his son, Imam Ali al-Rida (a.s.), promising seventy thousand accepted pilgrimages (*Hajjatun Maburah*) to distinguish it from the general Hajj which may be rejected. The comparison to 'visiting God at His Throne' is explained by Shaykh al-Saduq as a metaphor for proximity to the Divine Presence, drawing on the angelic tradition of circumambulating the Throne, rather than implying God's physical location. This underscores the Shia concept of the Imams as the ultimate locus of divine connection, where their descendants hold a unique rank among the Four from the First and the Four from the Last.
